title: Fertilization and the zygote — video support
purpose: Explain where fertilization normally occurs, how one sperm contributes its chromosomes, and how the diploid chromosome number is restored.
fallback: The sperm head has an acrosome containing enzymes that help it interact with and pass through the oocyte's surrounding layers. Reaching these layers is not yet the same as successfully fertilizing the cell. Membranes must interact and the sperm must contribute its contents. Fusion helps activate the oocyte. The oocyte completes meiosis II, and changes involving cortical granules modify the zona pellucida, the protective coat surrounding it. These changes help prevent additional sperm from entering. Do not imagine that many sperm are supposed to contribute chromosomes to one normal human zygote. The two chromosome contributions become associated with the developing cell's first division. For this chapter, focus on the result: one diploid cell containing genetic information from both gametes. The detailed chromosome movements will return in Chapter 16.

title: Fetal development and developmental influences — video support
purpose: Distinguish embryonic and fetal development, identify the age convention used, and explain how timing, dose and susceptibility affect developmental outcomes.
fallback: During early development, the main body plan and basic organs become established. During the fetal period, these structures grow and mature. Brain development, skeletal changes and lung maturation continue; the appearance of an organ does not mean it is ready for independent function. Pregnancy is also divided into three trimesters. These are broad time groupings, not three abrupt biological switches. Early pregnancy emphasizes establishment of structures; the middle and later periods include substantial growth and functional maturation. A developmental timeline helps organize changes, but individual milestones vary. Do not use a single classroom diagram to predict an individual fetus's exact capacity to survive outside the uterus.

title: Labour and birth as positive feedback — video support
purpose: Trace cervical stretch, neural signalling and oxytocin, then distinguish the three stages of parturition.
fallback: Stronger contractions can push the baby more firmly against the cervix, increasing stretch. That additional stretch promotes further signalling and oxytocin release. The response reinforces the initiating change instead of opposing it. This is why the loop is called positive feedback. The word positive does not mean “good.” It describes the relationship between response and stimulus. Compare negative feedback, in which a response reduces a deviation or decreases the signal that initiated it. Delivery removes much of the cervical-stretch stimulus from this particular loop. A feedback explanation is incomplete unless it identifies what ends or limits the amplification.
